analysis.investment_thesis: Aurionpro is a B2B technology company for banking infrastructure — outside my circle of competence in retail and consumer businesses — with dangerously low promoter skin-in-the-game at 26.88% and a FCF yield of barely 1.2% at current market cap. The near-zero debt is admirable, but this business fails too many of my core filters to warrant capital allocation.
key_strengths: Near debt-free balance sheet — D/E of 0.02 with borrowings down to just ₹30 Cr, financing costs collapsed from ₹23 Cr (2016) to ₹7 Cr (2025)
Accelerating recent financial performance — revenue grew from ₹374 Cr (2021) to ₹1,173 Cr (2025) and operating margins hold at 17.4%
OCF positive all 5 years (2021-2025), cash on hand ₹269 Cr providing cushion for ongoing acquisition strategy
key_risks: Promoter holding critically low at 26.88% — far below my 55% minimum; promoters have limited financial alignment with minority shareholders
FCF yield is only ~1.2% (₹62 Cr FCF on ₹5,094 Cr market cap) — well below my 5% threshold; FCF also volatile (negative in FY20, FY23)
Aggressive acquisition-driven expansion: investing CF was -₹421 Cr in FY25, funded by ₹283 Cr equity raise — dilutive and operationally risky
red_flags: Promoter holding at 26.88% — dangerously low, half my minimum threshold of 55%
FY2021 net loss of -₹192 Cr from impairments/write-offs reveals business model instability in that era
9-year revenue CAGR only 5.7% — revenue actually declined from ₹710 Cr (2016) to ₹374 Cr (2021); recovery is recent and acquisition-driven
Equity base ballooned from ₹337 Cr to ₹1,606 Cr in 4 years through equity raises — significant dilution risk for existing holders
B2B enterprise software for capital markets and smart cities — inherently lumpy, government-dependent revenues outside my domain
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aurionpro is a technically competent B2B software company serving banking, capital markets, and smart city clients, but it sits entirely outside the sectors I understand and trust — consumer retail, FMCG, and financial services with predictable end-customer demand. The most disqualifying factor is the 26.88% promoter holding. I have built my wealth by backing promoters who own large portions of their own businesses and behave like owners. At 26.88%, this promoter has little financial pain if the business deteriorates. The 9-year revenue CAGR of just 5.7% — with an actual contraction from FY16 to FY21 — tells me the underlying business has had structural struggles. The recent recovery looks impressive on paper, but it appears driven by acquisitions: investing cash outflow of ₹421 Cr in FY25 alone, funded by ₹283 Cr in new equity. That is not organic compounding — that is financial engineering.

The balance sheet cleanliness (D/E 0.02) is genuine and I respect it. Declining finance costs are also a good sign. But FCF conversion is weak — only ₹62 Cr of free cash flow on ₹188 Cr net profit in FY25, and negative FCF in two of the last five years. At a market cap of ₹5,094 Cr, the FCF yield is roughly 1.2%, versus my required 5%+. The P/E of 25x is above my comfort zone, and while the forward P/E of 17x is more palatable, I am not willing to pay for acquisitive growth stories in sectors I cannot evaluate deeply. For the patient, conservative capital I deploy, this is simply not the right vehicle.
